# css-animation-lab

> A research environment for CSS animation: 211 catalogued experiments, 34 findings
> recorded with explicit confidence levels, and a zero-dependency verifier that runs
> the CSS in a real browser. The point is not generating CSS animation — models
> already do that well. The point is **judging** it: telling whether the animation
> actually does anything, whether it is expensive, and whether it seams when it loops.

## What this is for

Writing a CSS animation is cheap. Knowing whether it works is not. An animation can
be syntactically perfect, pass every linter, and still produce **nothing at all** —
a misspelled `@keyframes` name, a property that never reaches paint, a `clip-path`
whose vertices are collinear. None of these raise an error. You only find out by
watching it, which does not scale.

This project moves that judgment to where it can be automated:

| Layer | What it decides | Who does it |
|---|---|---|
| Machine verification | Does it animate at all? Does the render change? Is it layout-bound? Does it seam? | scripts / this package |
| Filmstrip | Trajectory, overshoot, how early it arrives | read as still frames |
| Taste | Whether it feels good, whether it fits the moment | humans only |

Use the verifier before showing CSS animation to a user. A `fail`-level finding means
the animation is broken in a way that is invisible in code review.

## Verify CSS you wrote

```bash
npx css-animation-lab check anim.css --runtime
```

Exit code is 1 when any `fail`-level finding exists, so it drops into CI unchanged.
`--runtime` launches headless Chrome (no npm dependency; it borrows an installed
Chrome/Chromium, or the one at `$CHROME_PATH`). Without it, only static checks run.

Add `--json` for machine-readable output. Programmatic use:

```js
import { checkCss } from 'css-animation-lab';
const { findings, runtime } = await checkCss(css, { runtime: true });
// findings: [{ sev: 'fail'|'warn', rule, msg, why }]
// runtime:  { cost: 'compositor'|'paint'|'layout'|'unknown', properties, animationCount, cycleMs }
```

An MCP server exposing the same capability lives at `mcp/server.mjs`
(stdio, no SDK dependency). Tools: `check_css`, `search_catalog`,
`search_findings`, `get_patterns`.

## What the checks catch

Static (no browser needed) — each rule comes from a bug that was actually hit:

- a class name colliding with the harness's own layout names
- `sibling-index()` inside an unregistered custom property, read across elements
- `d:` on anything that is not a `<path>` (computes, never paints)
- a property written both statically and in `@keyframes` (the animation eats it)
- `clip-path: polygon()` with zero area (the element silently disappears)
- `pathLength` combined with `non-scaling-stroke` (dash lengths stop matching)
- asymmetric `border-radius` on a face that gets flipped 180°
- nested same-class elements spaced with `margin` (margins collapse; the parent moves)

Runtime (real browser):

- no animation was generated at all
- the rendered output is identical at every sampled point
- a visible jump at the loop boundary when the author intended seamlessness
- an element larger than its grid container being centred (centring silently fails)
- a stagger whose last element does not finish within one cycle
- an element following `offset-path` drifting off the drawn line
- cost classification: compositor / paint / layout, from the animated properties

## Resources

- [catalog.json](catalog.json): all 211 experiments, machine-readable. Each entry has
  `id`, `layer`, `axes` (technique / use / origin / target / timing), `predicted`, `note`.
- [FINDINGS.md](FINDINGS.md): 34 findings. Every one carries **claim**, **evidence**,
  **confidence** (`実測` measured / `仕様から確定` spec-derived / `仮説` hypothesis)
  and **effect**. Negative results are recorded with equal weight — that is the part
  the open web does not have.
- [PATTERNS.md](PATTERNS.md): the character of each motion type along three axes —
  attention cost, whether it reveals origin, and tolerance to repetition. Deliberately
  states no ranking; choosing is the caller's job.
- [BROWSER_SUPPORT.md](BROWSER_SUPPORT.md): measured per-browser behaviour, not
  caniuse tables.
- [README.md](README.md): how the lab works (Japanese).

## Layers in the catalog

- `L0` one property, one motion — the atoms
- `L2` composition patterns (simultaneous, lagged, split-easing, additive)
- `L3` stagger interval and ordering
- `L4` recipes fixed to a use case
- `T` techniques that combine CSS capabilities
- `E` expression borrowed from comics, film, optics

For `T` and `E`, index by `axes.technique` and `axes.use` rather than by motion name.

## Notes for models

- The catalog's `note` and `title` fields are Japanese; `title_en` and `note_en` carry
  English. Queries match against both.
- `predicted` is the author's prior guess (`good` / `uncertain` / `bad`), not a verdict.
  Do not present `predicted: good` as validated.
- Human verdicts live in `verdicts.json`. An empty `marks` means nothing has been
  judged by a person yet — say so rather than implying endorsement.
- The internal cycle in the lab is 1000ms. Individual animations may finish earlier
  or repeat within it, so `animation-duration` is only stated where it matters.
